solution:
On a **horizontal (unbanked)** curved road the only horizontal force available to supply the necessary centripetal force is the force of **static friction** between the tyres and the road. This is unsatisfactory for three reasons:

1. Friction has an upper limit, \(f_s \le \mu_s N\), which fixes an upper speed limit \(\text{v}_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}\).
2. \(\mu_s\) is not constant — the road surface is not uniform, and it falls sharply when the road is wet, oily or dusty, so the vehicle can skid.
3. Depending on friction also causes rapid wear of the tyres.

If the road surface is **tilted (banked)** through an angle \(\theta\) with the horizontal, the normal reaction \(N\) is no longer vertical. Its horizontal component \(N\sin\theta\) points **towards the centre** of the circular path and can itself provide the centripetal force, while \(N\cos\theta\) balances the weight:

\(N\sin\theta = \frac{m\text{v}^2}{r}\), \(N\cos\theta = mg\) \(\therefore \tan\theta = \frac{\text{v}^2}{rg}\)

At the **safest speed** \(\text{v} = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\) no friction at all is needed. Banking therefore makes the turn possible without depending on the unreliable force of friction, permits higher speeds and reduces wear of the tyres.

**Yes.** A two-wheeler needs a banked road just as much as a four-wheeler does — arguably more.

A two-wheeler cannot redistribute the normal reactions between an inner and an outer wheel the way a four-wheeler can, so on an unbanked road the rider is forced to **lean** into the turn through an angle \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\text{v}^2}{rg}\right)\) with the vertical, and the **whole** of the centripetal force must come from the force of static friction. If the road is wet or oily, \(\mu_s\) drops, the required friction is no longer available and the two-wheeler skids — with no second pair of wheels to fall back on.

On a banked road the horizontal component \(N\sin\theta\) of the normal reaction supplies part (or, at the safest speed \(\text{v} = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}\), all) of the centripetal force. The rider then has to lean much less, the demand on friction is reduced or removed, and the turn is safer.

Note also that the banking angle \(\tan\theta = \frac{\text{v}^2}{rg}\) and the leaning angle of the rider are given by the **same** expression, so a road banked for a given speed is exactly the road on which a rider travelling at that speed need not lean at all.

Because the moment of inertia depends **only on how the mass is distributed with respect to distance from the axis**, and not on the three-dimensional shape of the body. These two bodies happen to have the *same* radial mass distribution.

**Uniform disc** (surface density \(\sigma\), radius \(R\)), about its central axis: an elementary ring of radius \(r\) and width \(dr\) has mass

\(dm = \sigma(2\pi r\,dr) \propto r\,dr\)

**Uniform hollow right circular cone** (base radius \(R\), semi-vertical angle \(\alpha\)), about its central axis: the mass lies on the slanted surface. A ring of the surface at perpendicular distance \(r\) from the axis has circumference \(2\pi r\) and slant width \(ds = \frac{dr}{\sin\alpha}\), so its mass is

\(dm = \sigma\left(2\pi r \cdot \frac{dr}{\sin\alpha}\right) \propto r\,dr\)

In both bodies the mass of the elementary ring is proportional to \(r\,dr\) with the **same** limits \(r = 0\) to \(r = R\). Since

\(I = \int r^2\,dm\)

the two integrals are identical in form, and normalising by the total mass \(M\) in each case gives

\(I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\)

for both. The same reasoning is why a uniform disc and a **solid cylinder** also share \(\frac{1}{2}MR^2\) — stacking discs along the axis does not change any element's distance from that axis.

**Why the rider must lean.** On an unbanked (horizontal) circular road the centripetal force on a two-wheeler is supplied entirely by the force of static friction \(f_s\), which acts **horizontally at the road surface**, towards the centre. The weight \(mg\) acts at the centre of mass, which is a height \(h\) **above** the road. If the rider stayed upright, \(f_s\) (at the ground) and the centrifugal force in the rider's frame (at the centre of mass) would form a couple whose torque would topple the rider **outwards**. To prevent this the rider leans inwards, so that the **resultant of \(N\) and \(f_s\) passes through the centre of mass** and the net torque about the centre of mass is zero.

**Angle of leaning.** Let \(\theta\) be the angle of leaning with the vertical. Vertically and horizontally,

\(N = mg\) and \(f_s = \frac{m\text{v}^2}{r}\)

The resultant of \(N\) and \(f_s\) makes an angle \(\theta\) with the vertical such that

\(\tan\theta = \frac{f_s}{N} = \frac{m\text{v}^2/r}{mg}\)

\(\therefore \tan\theta = \frac{\text{v}^2}{rg}\) \(\therefore \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\text{v}^2}{rg}\right)\)

Note that \(\theta\) is independent of the mass of the rider and the vehicle, and is the **same expression as the banking angle**.

**Why a four-wheeler need not lean.** A four-wheeler has its wheels spread over a finite track width. The normal reactions on the inner and outer wheels can **redistribute themselves** — more of the load shifts to the outer wheels — and this unequal pair of normal forces supplies the balancing torque about the centre of mass. Its wheel base is wide and its centre of mass is low, so the toppling couple can be balanced without the body tilting at all.

Let a body of mass \(m\) be tied to a string of length \(r\) and whirled in a **vertical circle controlled only by gravity**. Take the lowermost point as the reference for potential energy.

**(a) Uppermost point.** Both the weight \(mg\) and the tension \(T_H\) point downwards, i.e. towards the centre:

\(T_H + mg = \frac{m\text{v}_H^2}{r}\) \(\therefore T_H = \frac{m\text{v}_H^2}{r} - mg\)

A string can only pull, so \(T_H \ge 0\). The least speed is the one for which the string just goes slack, \(T_H = 0\):

\(\boxed{(\text{v}_H)_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}}\)

**(b) Lowermost point.** The uppermost point is a height \(2r\) above the lowermost. By conservation of energy,

\(\frac{1}{2}m\text{v}_L^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\text{v}_H^2 + mg(2r)\) \(\therefore \text{v}_L^2 = \text{v}_H^2 + 4gr\)

Using \((\text{v}_H)_{\min}^2 = gr\):

\((\text{v}_L)_{\min} = \sqrt{gr + 4gr} = \sqrt{5gr}\)

**(c) Midway (string horizontal), a height \(r\) above the lowest point.**

\(\text{v}_M^2 = \text{v}_L^2 - 2gr = 5gr - 2gr = 3gr\) \(\therefore (\text{v}_M)_{\min} = \sqrt{3gr}\)

**Is zero speed possible at the uppermost point?** **Not** for motion controlled only by gravity along a *string* (or any flexible support). At \(\text{v} = 0\) no centripetal force is required, but the weight \(mg\) still acts downwards and is unbalanced, so the body would simply leave the circular path and fall. The speed there must be at least \(\sqrt{gr}\).

Zero speed at the top **is** possible if the body is attached to a **rigid rod** (or moves inside a groove or tube), because a rod can **push outwards** and support the weight. Then the minimum speed at the top is zero, and the corresponding minimum speed at the bottom is \(\sqrt{4gr} = 2\sqrt{gr}\).

**Difference between the extreme tensions.** At the lowest and highest points,

\(T_L - mg = \frac{m\text{v}_L^2}{r}\) \(\therefore T_L = mg + \frac{m\text{v}_L^2}{r}\)

\(T_H + mg = \frac{m\text{v}_H^2}{r}\) \(\therefore T_H = \frac{m\text{v}_H^2}{r} - mg\)

\(\therefore T_L - T_H = 2mg + \frac{m}{r}\left(\text{v}_L^2 - \text{v}_H^2\right)\)

But \(\text{v}_L^2 - \text{v}_H^2 = 4gr\) always, from energy conservation over the height \(2r\). Hence

\(T_L - T_H = 2mg + \frac{m(4gr)}{r} = 2mg + 4mg = 6mg\)

The difference is \(6mg\) — it depends **only upon the weight of the object**, and not on the radius, nor on the speed, nor on how fast the body is being whirled. The identical result \(N_L - N_H = 6mg\) holds for the normal forces in a sphere of death or a giant wheel.

**Necessity.** For a rigid body, \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\), which requires the distance of *every* mass element from the axis. For a body of complicated shape this is impractical, and the answer changes with every new axis. It is far more convenient to replace the actual distribution by a **single equivalent distance**.

**Definition.** The **radius of gyration** \(K\) of a body about a given axis is the distance from that axis at which, if the **entire mass \(M\)** of the body were concentrated as a point, its moment of inertia would equal the actual moment of inertia of the body:

\(I = MK^2\) \(\therefore K = \sqrt{\frac{I}{M}}\)

**It depends on:**

- the **distribution of mass** about the axis — that is, the shape and size of the body;
- the **position and orientation of the axis** of rotation (a disc has \(K = \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\) about its central axis but \(K = \frac{R}{2}\) about a diameter).

**It does not depend on:**

- the **mass** of the body. For a body of given shape \(I \propto M\), so \(M\) cancels in \(K = \sqrt{I/M}\); a wooden disc and an iron disc of the same radius have the same \(K\);
- the angular speed, the torque applied, or the state of motion.

**Similarity with the centre of mass.** Both replace an extended body by a single equivalent quantity. The **centre of mass** is the point at which the whole mass may be taken to be concentrated for **translational** dynamics; the **radius of gyration** is the distance at which the whole mass may be taken to be concentrated for **rotational** dynamics about a given axis. Both are fixed by the mass *distribution* and are independent of the total mass, and neither need lie on the material of the body (both lie in empty space for a ring).

**If a uniform ring and a uniform disc have the same radius of gyration.** Equal \(K\) means equal \(\frac{I}{M}\), so if their masses are also equal they have equal moments of inertia — the two behave identically in rotation, acquiring the same angular acceleration under the same torque. Taking both about their central axes, \(K_{\text{ring}} = R_{\text{ring}}\) while \(K_{\text{disc}} = \frac{R_{\text{disc}}}{\sqrt{2}}\), so

\(R_{\text{ring}} = \frac{R_{\text{disc}}}{\sqrt{2}}\) \(\therefore R_{\text{disc}} = \sqrt{2}\,R_{\text{ring}}\)

that is, the disc must be \(\sqrt{2}\) times as large in radius as the ring — which is only to be expected, since a disc has much of its mass closer to the axis.

**Theorem of parallel axes.**

*Conditions:* It applies to **any** body — laminar or three-dimensional, of any shape. The two axes must be **parallel** to each other, and **one of them must pass through the centre of mass** of the body.

*Statement and expression:* The moment of inertia of a body about any axis is the sum of its moment of inertia about a parallel axis through its centre of mass and the product of its mass with the square of the perpendicular distance between the two axes.

\(I_o = I_c + Mh^2\)

where \(I_c\) is the moment of inertia about the axis through the centre of mass, \(M\) the mass of the body and \(h\) the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.

**Theorem of perpendicular axes.**

*Conditions:* It applies **only to a laminar (plane, two-dimensional) object**. The three axes must be **mutually perpendicular and concurrent**, with two of them (\(x\) and \(y\)) lying **in the plane** of the lamina and the third (\(z\)) **perpendicular to that plane**.

*Statement and expression:* The moment of inertia of a laminar object about an axis perpendicular to its plane is the sum of its moments of inertia about two mutually perpendicular axes in its plane, all three being concurrent.

\(I_z = I_x + I_y\)

Consider a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity \(\omega\). Imagine the body to be made of \(N\) particles of masses \(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_N\) situated at perpendicular distances \(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_N\) from the axis.

Every particle of a rigid body has the **same angular velocity** \(\omega\), so the linear speed of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) particle is

\(\text{v}_i = r_i\omega\)

and its linear momentum is \(p_i = m_i\text{v}_i = m_i r_i \omega\), directed along the tangent, i.e. **perpendicular** to \(\vec{r_i}\).

Its angular momentum about the axis is therefore

\(L_i = r_i p_i \sin 90^\circ = r_i (m_i r_i \omega) = m_i r_i^2 \omega\)

For a body rotating about a fixed axis all these angular momenta are along the same direction (the axis), so they add as scalars:

\(L = \sum_{i=1}^{N} L_i = \left(m_1 r_1^2 + m_2 r_2^2 + \cdots + m_N r_N^2\right)\omega\)

\(\therefore L = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_i r_i^2\right)\omega\)

But \(\sum m_i r_i^2 = I\), the moment of inertia of the body about that axis. Hence

\(L = I\omega\)

This is the rotational analogue of \(p = m\text{v}\), with \(I\) replacing mass and \(\omega\) replacing linear velocity.

Consider a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular acceleration \(\alpha\). Imagine it to be made of \(N\) particles of masses \(m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_N\) at perpendicular distances \(r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_N\) from the axis.

Every particle of a rigid body has the **same angular acceleration** \(\alpha\), so the tangential (linear) acceleration of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) particle is

\(a_i = r_i\alpha\)

The tangential force needed to produce it is

\(f_i = m_i a_i = m_i r_i \alpha\)

This force acts perpendicular to \(\vec{r_i}\), so the torque it exerts about the axis is

\(\tau_i = f_i \, r_i \sin 90^\circ = m_i r_i^2 \alpha\)

All such torques are along the same direction (the axis of rotation), so the total torque is their scalar sum:

\(\tau = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tau_i = \left(m_1 r_1^2 + m_2 r_2^2 + \cdots + m_N r_N^2\right)\alpha = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} m_i r_i^2\right)\alpha\)

\(\therefore \tau = I\alpha\)

where \(I\) is the moment of inertia of the body about the given axis.

This is the rotational analogue of \(f = ma\), and it is the **physical significance of moment of inertia**: \(I\) measures the opposition a body offers to a change in its rotational motion, exactly as mass measures the opposition to a change in translational motion.

**Statement.** The angular momentum of a body (or a system of bodies) remains **constant in magnitude and direction** if the **net external torque** acting upon it is zero.

**Explanation.** From the relation between torque and angular momentum,

\(\vec{\tau} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}\)

If \(\vec{\tau} = 0\), then \(\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = 0\), so \(\vec{L} = \) constant. For rotation about a fixed axis this means

\(L = I\omega = I(2\pi n) = \) constant

Hence \(I\) and \(n\) are **inversely** related: if the moment of inertia is increased, the angular speed and the frequency of revolution decrease; if the moment of inertia is decreased, the frequency increases. Note that the body itself may change shape — only the *external* torque has to vanish.

**Illustration — a ballet dancer (or an ice skater).** While spinning, the dancer draws the arms and the outstretched leg close to the axis of rotation. This brings the mass nearer the axis, so \(I\) becomes **minimum** and, since \(I\omega\) is constant, the spin becomes noticeably **faster**. To slow down before stopping, the dancer stretches the arms and legs outwards, increasing \(I\) and reducing \(\omega\) — which also reduces the linear speed of the feet and prevents slipping. The friction at the skate is along the axis and exerts almost no torque about it, which is why \(L\) is conserved.

**Do we use it in daily life? When?** Yes:

- A **diver** in a swimming pool stretches the body on the board (large \(I\)), folds it immediately after leaving the board to reduce \(I\) sharply and complete more somersaults in the air, then stretches out again for a smooth, streamlined entry into the water.
- An **acrobat in a circus** and a gymnast use the same trick while tumbling.
- A person sitting on a **rotating stool** with weights in the hands spins faster on folding the arms in and slower on stretching them out.

Consider a body of mass \(M\), radius \(R\) and radius of gyration \(K\) rolling **without slipping** with its centre of mass moving at speed \(\text{v}\). Rolling without slipping means

\(\omega = \frac{\text{v}}{R}\), and \(I = MK^2\)

The motion is the sum of a pure translation of the centre of mass and a pure rotation about the central axis, so the body possesses **two** kinetic energies:

Translational K.E. \(= \frac{1}{2}M\text{v}^2\)

Rotational K.E. \(= \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(MK^2\right)\left(\frac{\text{v}}{R}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}M\text{v}^2\cdot\frac{K^2}{R^2}\)

Total K.E. \(= \frac{1}{2}M\text{v}^2\left(1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)\)

**The interlink.** Dividing,

\(\frac{\text{Rotational K.E.}}{\text{Translational K.E.}} = \frac{K^2}{R^2}\)

This is a **pure number fixed entirely by the shape** of the body — it does not depend on the mass, the radius or the speed. Consequently

Translational : Rotational : Total \(= 1 : \frac{K^2}{R^2} : \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)\)

and the fractions of the total energy are

\(\frac{\text{Translational}}{\text{Total}} = \frac{1}{1 + K^2/R^2}\), \(\frac{\text{Rotational}}{\text{Total}} = \frac{K^2/R^2}{1 + K^2/R^2}\)

| Body | \(\frac{K^2}{R^2}\) | Trans : Rot : Total |
|---|---|---|
| Ring or thin walled hollow cylinder | 1 | 1 : 1 : 2 |
| Disc or solid cylinder | \(\frac{1}{2}\) | 2 : 1 : 3 |
| Solid sphere | \(\frac{2}{5}\) | 5 : 2 : 7 |
| Thin walled hollow sphere | \(\frac{2}{3}\) | 3 : 2 : 5 |

Thus for a ring exactly **half** the total energy is rotational, while for a solid sphere only \(\frac{2}{7}\) of it is. The larger \(\frac{K^2}{R^2}\) is, the greater the share of the energy locked up in rotation, and the less is available for translation — which is why a ring rolls down an incline more slowly than a sphere of the same mass and radius.

Let an object of mass \(M\), radius \(R\) and radius of gyration \(K\) roll **without slipping** from rest down a plane inclined at \(\theta\) to the horizontal. Let it travel a distance \(s\) along the incline, falling through a vertical height

\(h = s\sin\theta\)

**Speed after falling through a height \(h\).** In pure rolling the point of contact is instantaneously at rest, so the force of static friction does **no work** and the total mechanical energy is conserved. All the loss of gravitational potential energy appears as kinetic energy:

\(Mgh = \frac{1}{2}M\text{v}^2\left(1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)\)

\(\therefore \text{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gs\sin\theta}{1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}}}\)

**Acceleration along the track.** Since the object starts from rest and the acceleration is uniform, \(\text{v}^2 = 2as\):

\(a = \frac{\text{v}^2}{2s} = \frac{1}{2s}\cdot\frac{2gs\sin\theta}{1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}}\)

\(\therefore a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \dfrac{K^2}{R^2}}\)

**Discussion.** Both \(a\) and \(\text{v}\) are **independent of the mass \(M\) and of the radius \(R\)**; they depend on the body only through the shape factor \(\frac{K^2}{R^2}\). The smaller that factor, the larger the acceleration and the final speed — so among bodies released together from the same height a solid sphere \(\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\) arrives first, then a disc \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\), then a hollow sphere \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\), and a ring \(\left(1\right)\) last. For a body sliding without rolling, \(\frac{K^2}{R^2} = 0\) and we recover \(a = g\sin\theta\), the largest possible value.

**Data:** \(n_0 = 0\), \(n = 2\) rev/s, \(t = 10\) s, uniform angular acceleration.

Since every quantity asked for is a number of revolutions or a time, it is simplest to use the **revolution** as the unit of angle throughout — then \(\pi\) never appears. (The diameter of 1 m is not needed for either part; it would matter only for the ant's linear speed.)

\(\alpha = \frac{n - n_0}{t} = \frac{2 - 0}{10} = 0.2\ \text{rev/s}^2\)

**(i) Number of revolutions in 10 s.**

\(N = n_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 = 0 + \frac{1}{2}(0.2)(10)^2 = 10\ \text{revolutions}\)

**(ii) Time for the first complete revolution.** Put \(N = 1\) with \(n_0 = 0\):

\(1 = \frac{1}{2}(0.2)t_{\text{first}}^2\) \(\therefore t_{\text{first}}^2 = 10\) \(\therefore t_{\text{first}} = \sqrt{10} = 3.162\ \text{s}\)

**Time for the last complete revolution.** The last (tenth) revolution runs from \(N = 9\) to \(N = 10\). Time to complete 9 revolutions:

\(9 = \frac{1}{2}(0.2)t_9^2\) \(\therefore t_9 = \sqrt{90} = 9.4868\ \text{s}\)

The tenth revolution is complete at \(t = 10\) s, so

\(t_{\text{last}} = 10 - 9.4868 = 0.5132\ \text{s}\)

**Answers:** 10 revolutions; \(t_{\text{first}} = \sqrt{10} = 3.162\) s and \(t_{\text{last}} = 0.5132\) s. The last revolution takes about **one sixth** of the time of the first, because the wheel has been speeding up throughout.

**Data:** \(\mu_s = 0.5\), disc radius \(= 8\) cm, initial position of the coin \(r_1 = 2\ \text{cm} = 0.02\) m, \(g = \pi^2\ \text{m/s}^2\) (as the stem specifies).

The coin moves in a horizontal circle, so the centripetal force must be supplied by the force of static friction between the coin and the disc. It stays put only while

\(mr\omega^2 \le \mu_s mg\) \(\therefore \omega^2 \le \frac{\mu_s g}{r}\)

With \(\omega = 2\pi n\), the coin begins to slip at the frequency

\(n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_s g}{r}}\)

**At \(r_1 = 0.02\) m:**

\(n_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{0.5 \times \pi^2}{0.02}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{25\pi^2} = \frac{5\pi}{2\pi} = 2.5\ \text{rev/s}\)

**At the rim,** \(r_2 = 8\ \text{cm} = 4r_1\). Since \(n \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}\) with everything else unchanged,

\(\frac{n_2}{n_1} = \sqrt{\frac{r_1}{r_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore n_2 = \frac{1}{2}n_1 = 1.25\ \text{rev/s}\)

**Answers:** the coin starts slipping at a minimum frequency of **2.5 rev/s**, and at the rim the answer is **halved** — \(n_2 = \frac{1}{2}n_1 = 1.25\) rev/s. A coin further from the centre needs a *smaller* frequency to be flung off, because the required centripetal force grows with \(r\) while the available friction does not.

**Data:** \(r = 72\) m, maximum speed \(\text{v} = 216\) kmph, width of track \(w = 10\) m, \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\).

\(\text{v} = 216 \times \frac{5}{18} = 60\ \text{m/s}\)

**Angle of banking.** The track should be banked for this speed so that no friction is needed:

\(\tan\theta = \frac{\text{v}^2}{rg} = \frac{(60)^2}{72 \times 10} = \frac{3600}{720} = 5\)

\(\therefore \theta = \tan^{-1}(5) = 78.69^\circ\)

**Height of the outer edge.** The road surface is the width of the track, inclined at \(\theta\) to the horizontal. The outer edge is raised above the inner edge by

\(h = w\sin\theta = 10 \times \sin 78.69^\circ = 10 \times 0.9806\)

\(\therefore h = 9.806 \cong 9.8\ \text{m}\)

**Answers:** the road should be tilted at \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(5) = 78.69^\circ\), and the outer edge should be about **9.8 m** above the inner edge.

(This is a very steeply banked track — nearly 79° — which is why such banking is found only on special racing tracks and not on ordinary highways.)

**Data (from Q.14):** \(r = 72\) m, \(\theta = 78.69^\circ\) so \(\tan\theta = 5\), \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\), and now \(\mu_s = 0.8\).

**Lower speed limit.** \(\text{v}_{\min} = \sqrt{rg\left(\dfrac{\tan\theta - \mu_s}{1 + \mu_s\tan\theta}\right)}\)

\(= \sqrt{72 \times 10 \left(\frac{5 - 0.8}{1 + 0.8 \times 5}\right)} = \sqrt{720 \times \frac{4.2}{5}} = \sqrt{604.8}\)

\(\therefore \text{v}_{\min} = 24.59\ \text{m/s} = 24.59 \times 3.6 = 88.53 \cong 88\ \text{kmph}\)

**Yes, there is a lower speed limit** — about 88 kmph. Below it the vehicle slides *down* the steep slope towards the inner edge. (A lower limit exists here because \(\mu_s = 0.8 < \tan\theta = 5\); on an ordinary gently banked road \(\mu_s \ge \tan\theta\) and \(\text{v}_{\min} = 0\).)

**Upper speed limit.** \(\text{v}_{\max} = \sqrt{rg\left(\dfrac{\tan\theta + \mu_s}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}\right)}\)

Here the denominator is

\(1 - \mu_s\tan\theta = 1 - (0.8)(5) = -3\)

which is **negative**, so the formula yields no finite real speed. The condition for \(\text{v}_{\max} \to \infty\) is \(\mu_s \ge \cot\theta\), and here \(\cot\theta = \frac{1}{5} = 0.2\) while \(\mu_s = 0.8\), so the condition is comfortably met.

**Therefore there is no upper speed limit at all** — the road is banked at \(\theta = 78.69^\circ > 45^\circ\), and the inward components of the normal reaction and of the friction can together supply the centripetal force for *any* speed. The upper limit can be exceeded by **any** amount, so far as skidding outwards is concerned. (In practice other factors — the strength of the tyres, the engine, and the ability of the driver to withstand the large normal force — set the real limit.)

**Data:** \(r = 6.05\) m, \(\mu_s = 0.5\), \(m = 50\) kg, \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\).

Inside a **vertical cylindrical wall** the normal reaction \(N\) is horizontal and supplies the whole centripetal force, while the only upward force available to balance the weight is the **vertically upward force of static friction** \(f_s\):

\(N = \frac{m\text{v}^2}{r}\) and \(f_s = mg\)

**Minimum speed.** Since \(f_s \le \mu_s N\),

\(mg \le \mu_s\frac{m\text{v}^2}{r}\) \(\therefore \text{v}^2 \ge \frac{rg}{\mu_s}\)

\(\therefore \text{v}_{\min} = \sqrt{\frac{rg}{\mu_s}} = \sqrt{\frac{6.05 \times 10}{0.5}} = \sqrt{121} = 11\ \text{m/s}\)

**Force of friction after a 20 % increase in speed.**

\(\text{v} = 1.2 \times 11 = 13.2\ \text{m/s}\)

The friction is **static**, so its value is not \(\mu_s N\) — it is only as large as it needs to be. The artist does not move vertically, so the friction must exactly balance the weight, whatever the speed:

\(f_s = mg = 50 \times 10 = 500\ \text{N}\)

**The force of friction does not change: it stays 500 N.** What the extra speed buys is a bigger safety margin — the normal reaction rises to \(N = \frac{50 \times (13.2)^2}{6.05} = 1440\) N, so the *limiting* friction rises to \(\mu_s N = 720\) N, comfortably above the 500 N actually required (at the minimum speed the two were exactly equal).

**Data:** \(L = 20\ \text{cm} = 0.2\) m, \(m = 100\ \text{g} = 0.1\) kg, \(n = 75\ \text{rpm} = 1.25\) rev/s, \(\pi^2 = 10\) (given), \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\).

\(\omega^2 = (2\pi n)^2 = 4\pi^2 n^2 = 4(10)(1.25)^2 = 62.5\ \text{rad}^2/\text{s}^2\)

**Semi-vertical angle.** For a conical pendulum with the string at \(\theta\) to the vertical, the radius of the horizontal circle is \(r = L\sin\theta\), and

\(T\cos\theta = mg\), \(T\sin\theta = mr\omega^2 = mL\sin\theta\,\omega^2\)

\(\therefore \cos\theta = \frac{g}{L\omega^2} = \frac{10}{0.2 \times 62.5} = \frac{10}{12.5} = 0.8\)

\(\therefore \sin\theta = 0.6\)

**Kinetic energy.**

\(r = L\sin\theta = 0.2 \times 0.6 = 0.12\ \text{m}\)

\(\text{v} = r\omega\) \(\therefore \text{v}^2 = r^2\omega^2 = (0.12)^2 \times 62.5 = 0.9\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2\)

\(\therefore \text{K.E.} = \frac{1}{2}m\text{v}^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.1)(0.9) = 0.045\ \text{J}\)

**Increase in gravitational potential energy.** The bob has risen above its rest position (string vertical) by

\(h = L - L\cos\theta = L(1 - \cos\theta) = 0.2(1 - 0.8) = 0.04\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore \Delta(\text{P.E.}) = mgh = 0.1 \times 10 \times 0.04 = 0.04\ \text{J}\)

**Answers:** \(\cos\theta = 0.8\), K.E. \(= 0.045\) J, and the gain in gravitational P.E. \(= 0.04\) J (an **increase**, since the bob rises).

A useful check on the K.E.: for a conical pendulum \(\tan\theta = \frac{\text{v}^2}{rg}\), so \(\text{v}^2 = rg\tan\theta = 0.12 \times 10 \times \frac{0.6}{0.8} = 0.9\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2\), giving the same 0.045 J by an independent route.

**Data:** inside a sphere of death the speed is greatest at the lowest point and least at the highest, so \(\text{v}_L = 10\) m/s, \(\text{v}_H = 6\) m/s, \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\). Let \(r\) be the radius of the sphere.

**Diameter.** The highest point is a height \(2r\) above the lowest, so by conservation of energy

\(\frac{1}{2}m\text{v}_L^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\text{v}_H^2 + mg(2r)\) \(\therefore \text{v}_L^2 - \text{v}_H^2 = 4gr\)

\((10)^2 - (6)^2 = 4(10)r\) \(\therefore 100 - 36 = 40r\) \(\therefore 64 = 40r\)

\(\therefore r = 1.6\ \text{m}\) \(\therefore \text{Diameter} = 2r = 3.2\ \text{m}\)

**Minimum possible values of the two speeds.** For this radius, the least speed at the uppermost point is the one at which the normal reaction just vanishes:

\((\text{v}_H)_{\min} = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{10 \times 1.6} = \sqrt{16} = 4\ \text{m/s}\)

and the corresponding least speed at the lowermost point is

\((\text{v}_L)_{\min} = \sqrt{5gr} = \sqrt{80} = 4\sqrt{5} = 8.94\ \text{m/s}\)

**Answers:** diameter \(= 3.2\) m; minimum possible speeds \((\text{v}_1)_{\min} = 4\) m/s at the top and \((\text{v}_2)_{\min} = 4\sqrt{5} \cong 8.94\) m/s at the bottom. The rider's actual speeds (6 m/s and 10 m/s) are both safely above these minima.

**Data:** ring of mass \(M = 1\) kg, moment of inertia about **one of its diameters** \(= 1\ \text{kg m}^2\).

**Step 1 — find the radius.** For a ring about its central axis \(I_z = MR^2\). The ring is a lamina, so by the theorem of perpendicular axes with the two in-plane axes being any two perpendicular diameters,

\(I_z = I_x + I_y = 2I_{\text{diameter}}\) \(\therefore I_{\text{diameter}} = \frac{1}{2}MR^2\)

\(\therefore \frac{1}{2}(1)R^2 = 1\) \(\therefore R^2 = 2\ \text{m}^2\)

**Step 2 — the disc.** Melting and remoulding conserves the **mass**, so the disc also has \(M = 1\) kg, and it is given the **same radius**, \(R^2 = 2\ \text{m}^2\). About its **own axis** (central, perpendicular to its plane) a uniform disc has

\(I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 = \frac{1}{2}(1)(2) = 1\ \text{kg m}^2\)

**Answer:** \(I = 1\ \text{kg m}^2\) — numerically unchanged.

Note that this equality is a coincidence of the two axes chosen, not a general rule: the ring's value was quoted about a **diameter** (\(\frac{1}{2}MR^2\)) while the disc's is about its **own central axis** (also \(\frac{1}{2}MR^2\)). Had the ring's value been quoted about its own axis it would have been \(MR^2\), i.e. twice as large.

Moment of inertia is \(\text{mass} \times (\text{length})^2\), so the unit is \(\text{g cm}^2\); as printed the quantity has dimensions \(\text{M L}^{-2}\), which is not a moment of inertia at all.]

**Data:** rod \(M = 60\) g, \(L = 20\) cm; two solid spheres \(m = 25\) g, \(R = 10\) cm each, at the two **ends** of the rod. The axis passes through the centre of the rod and is perpendicular to its length. Work throughout in g and cm.

**Rod.** About a transverse axis through its centre,

\(I_{\text{rod}} = \frac{ML^2}{12} = \frac{60 \times (20)^2}{12} = \frac{24000}{12} = 2000\ \text{g cm}^2\)

**Each sphere.** Its centre sits at the end of the rod, so the distance of its centre from the axis is

\(d = \frac{L}{2} + R = 10 + 10 = 20\ \text{cm}\)

A solid sphere about its own diameter has \(\frac{2}{5}mR^2\); shifting to the parallel axis through the centre of the dumb-bell requires the **theorem of parallel axes**:

\(I_{\text{sphere}} = \frac{2}{5}mR^2 + md^2 = \frac{2}{5}(25)(10)^2 + 25(20)^2\)

\(= 1000 + 10000 = 11000\ \text{g cm}^2\)

**Both spheres:** \(2 \times 11000 = 22000\ \text{g cm}^2\)

**Total.**

\(I = I_{\text{rod}} + 2I_{\text{sphere}} = 2000 + 22000 = 24000\ \text{g cm}^2\)

**Answer:** \(I = 24000\ \text{g cm}^2 = 2.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^2\).

Note that the spheres contribute more than **90 %** of the total, and that most of their contribution comes from the \(md^2\) shift rather than from their own \(\frac{2}{5}mR^2\). Moment of inertia has dimensions of \(\text{mass} \times (\text{length})^2\), so the unit is \(\text{g cm}^2\).

**Data:** flywheel (a uniform disc) \(M = 10\) kg, \(R = 0.4\) m, \(n_1 = 100\) rpm; clay \(m = 1.6\) kg lands at a distance \(x\) from the centre; \(n_2 = 80\) rpm.

**Moment of inertia of the flywheel.**

\(I_1 = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 = \frac{1}{2}(10)(0.4)^2 = 0.8\ \text{kg m}^2\)

**After the clay adheres,** treating the lump as a particle at distance \(x\),

\(I_2 = I_1 + mx^2 = 0.8 + 1.6x^2\)

**Conservation of angular momentum.** The clay falls **vertically** and sticks, so it exerts no torque about the vertical axis of rotation; there is no other external torque, hence \(L\) is conserved:

\(I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2\) \(\therefore I_1(2\pi n_1) = I_2(2\pi n_2)\) \(\therefore I_1 n_1 = I_2 n_2\)

(The frequencies may be left in rpm, since only their ratio matters.)

\(0.8 \times 100 = (0.8 + 1.6x^2) \times 80\)

\(80 = 64 + 128x^2\) \(\therefore 128x^2 = 16\) \(\therefore x^2 = 0.125 = \frac{1}{8}\)

\(\therefore x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}} = 0.3536 \cong 0.35\ \text{m}\)

**Answer:** \(x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\ \text{m} \cong 0.35\) m from the centre. As expected the frequency **decreased**, because adding the clay increased the moment of inertia while \(I\omega\) stayed constant.

**Data:** the incline rises 3 units for every 5 units measured **along** it, so

\(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}\)

The object starts from rest, rolls without slipping, and gains \(\text{v} = \sqrt{10}\ \text{m/s}\) over a distance \(s = \frac{5}{3}\) m along the incline; \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2\).

**Vertical height fallen.**

\(h = s\sin\theta = \frac{5}{3} \times \frac{3}{5} = 1\ \text{m}\)

**Energy conservation** (in pure rolling the static friction does no work):

\(Mgh = \frac{1}{2}M\text{v}^2\left(1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2}\right)\)

\(\therefore 1 + \frac{K^2}{R^2} = \frac{2gh}{\text{v}^2} = \frac{2 \times 10 \times 1}{10} = 2\)

\(\therefore \frac{K^2}{R^2} = 1\) \(\therefore K = R\) \(\therefore I = MK^2 = MR^2\)

**Answer:** the shape factor is \(\frac{K^2}{R^2} = 1\), i.e. the whole of the mass behaves as though it were at the rim. The bodies with \(I = MR^2\) about the rolling axis are a **uniform ring** and a **thin walled hollow cylinder**.

Note that mass and radius cancel out completely — the answer identifies the *shape* alone, and no measurement of \(M\) or \(R\) could narrow it further. (A disc or solid cylinder would have given \(\frac{K^2}{R^2} = \frac{1}{2}\), and a solid sphere \(\frac{2}{5}\).)
